key_concept: The reaction centre of each photosystem is a special molecule of chlorophyll $a$; in PS I it absorbs maximally at $700\ \text{nm}$ and is called P700, while in PS II it absorbs at $680\ \text{nm}$ and is called P680.
steps: Each photosystem has two parts: a light-harvesting complex (antenna) and a single reaction centre.
The antenna contains chlorophyll $b$, xanthophylls and carotenoids. These accessory pigments absorb light and pass the energy to the reaction centre.
The reaction centre is the only pigment that actually loses an electron and drives the light reaction. In both photosystems it is a special form of chlorophyll $a$.
In PS I, this chlorophyll $a$ molecule has its absorption peak at $700\ \text{nm}$, hence the name P700. In PS II, the peak is at $680\ \text{nm}$, hence P680.
So the pigment at the P700 reaction centre is chlorophyll $a$, which matches the official answer, option (2).
why_not_others: Chlorophyll $b$, xanthophylls and carotenoids are all accessory pigments in the antenna complex. They only harvest light and transfer energy; none of them forms the reaction centre. Also, carotenoids and xanthophylls absorb mainly in the blue-green region ($400$–$500\ \text{nm}$), not at $700\ \text{nm}$.
common_trap: Students may think the "700" belongs to a different pigment from the one in PS II, or that it is chlorophyll $b$. In fact, both P700 and P680 are chlorophyll $a$; they differ only in their protein environment.
time_saving_tip: Remember the rule: reaction centre = chlorophyll $a$ (the primary pigment), and every other pigment = accessory. Any question about P680 or P700 then answers itself as chlorophyll $a$.
